snp1.3:1.4: The commentary (Nd II) describes several senses in which a solitary sage 'wanders alone': physically, by going forth without a companion and traveling unaccompanied; and mentally, through having abandoned craving, being free of passion, aversion, and delusion, and following what is called the 'path going one way only.' The commentary defines this path not simply as the four establishings of mindfulness (compare DN 22) but as the full set of seven groups of qualities making up the Wings to Awakening. It illustrates the abandoning-of-craving point with a verse paralleling Iti 15, and the one-way-path point with a verse paralleling SN 47:18 and SN 47:43.
snp1.3:5.1: SN 35:191 speaks of two fetters — desire and passion — while AN 10:13 gives a longer list of ten: views about self-identity, doubt, clinging to rules and observances, sensual desire, ill will, passion for form, passion for the formless, conceit, restlessness, and ignorance.
snp1.3:10.1: 'The householder's marks' refers to hair and beard.
snp1.3:12.4: These two lines correspond to Dhammapada verses 328–329.
snp1.3:16.3: 'Strings of sensuality' traditionally refers to pleasing sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and tactile sensations linked with desire, encountered through the five senses. Strictly speaking these objects themselves aren't 'sensuality' as such, but in technical usage they are called the 'strings' of sensuality. See AN 6:63.
snp1.3:20.2: 'Momentary release' refers to the temporary freedom from the hindrances gained upon entering right concentration, or the temporary freedom from certain factors of a lower jhāna gained upon reaching a higher one — a release that lasts only as long as the supporting conditions remain in place. This appears to be equivalent to the 'occasional release' mentioned in MN 29 (see that sutta's second note).
snp1.3:20.3: 'Kinsman of the Sun' is an epithet for the Buddha.
snp1.3:21.1: The commentary (Nd II) identifies 'views' here as the twenty forms of identity-view (see SN 22:1) together with the sixty-two views described in DN 1 (their relationship is discussed at SN 41:3). MN 2, however, explains the phrase 'contortion of views' somewhat differently, and that alternate sense may be what's intended here.
snp1.3:23.2: On the term rendered 'discordant' (visama), see the corresponding note at Sn 1:12.
snp1.3:27.3: A textual variant: the Thai editions read 'gaṇḍo' (tumor/boil, as translated here), while other editions have 'gaḷo' (fishhook). See AN 9:15.
snp1.3:29.3: Drawing on Nd II's citation of Ven. Mahā Moggallāna at SN 35:202: being 'soggy' describes a mind caught up in attraction to pleasant sights (and correspondingly for the other senses) or aversion to unpleasant ones, lacking mindfulness of the body and full awareness, so that unskillful states that arise aren't seen through to their cessation. Being 'not soggy' is the reverse — mindfulness of the body is present, awareness is unlimited, and one discerns the release of unskillful states through awareness and discernment. See also AN 3:110. 'Not burning' is explained as not burning with the fires of passion, aversion, and delusion; see SN 35:28 and Iti 93.
snp1.3:30.1: Here 'the householder's marks' refers to lay clothing (contrast the earlier occurrence at 10.1, referring to hair and beard).
snp1.3:33.3: This refers to the fourth jhāna; see MN 119.
snp1.3:37.3: These same lines recur at Sn 1:12.
snp1.3:41.5: See also: SN 21:10; SN 35:63; AN 9:40; Ud 4:5; Iti 15; Iti 38.
